01-logic-computability.purpose: Define what a mechanical procedure can do before asking what changes in quantum computing.
01-logic-computability.before: No formal logic is assumed. Be comfortable following a short algebraic argument.
outcomes: Separate checking, searching, and deciding.
Explain a Turing-machine configuration.
Distinguish determinism from reversibility.
01-logic-computability.limits: The halting theorem concerns a general always-correct terminating procedure; it does not prevent analyzing individual programs.
01-logic-computability.example: Follow Euclid’s algorithm: the answer is preserved even though distinct inputs can merge.
01-logic-computability.next: Chapter 2 replaces such information-losing steps with reversible constructions.

exercises.question: A proof search over a three-symbol alphabet has checked every candidate of length at most \(10\), including the empty string, without finding a proof. How many candidates is that, and what does the failure establish?
hints: There are \(3^k\) strings of length \(k\).
Unprovability is a claim about proofs of every length.
exercises.answer: \(1+3+\dots+3^{10}=(3^{11}-1)/2=88{,}573\) candidates. The failure shows only that the statement has no proof of length at most \(10\). A longer proof may exist, and no finite search can establish that none does.

exercises.question: A Turing machine is paused mid-run. You are told the tape contents \(\square111\square\) and that the head is on the second \(1\), but not the control state. The machine has states \(q_0\) (moving right over ones) and \(q_1\) (moving left back to the start). Can you resume the computation? What must a configuration contain?
hints: Would the next step be the same in \(q_0\) and in \(q_1\)?
A configuration must determine the next step without extra information.
exercises.answer: No. In \(q_0\) the next step moves the head right; in \(q_1\) it moves left. The tape and head position alone leave the next step undetermined. A configuration of a Turing machine is the triple of tape contents, head position, and control state, which together are exactly enough to resume. For Euclid’s algorithm, paused at the start of its repeated step, the pair alone sufficed because the next instruction was always the same. What a configuration must include depends on where the computation is allowed to pause.

exercises.question: The rule \(n\mapsto\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) (halve and round down) acts on the numbers \(0,1,\dots,7\). Is it deterministic? Is it one-to-one? Show how to keep one extra bit so that the step can be undone, and say what that bit records.
hints: Which pairs of inputs give the same output?
The lost information is whether \(n\) was even or odd.
exercises.answer: It is deterministic: each \(n\) has exactly one result. It is not one-to-one: \(2k\) and \(2k+1\) both go to \(k\), so \(0,1\mapsto0\), \(2,3\mapsto1\), and so on. Keep the remainder \(n\bmod2\) as an extra bit: \(n\mapsto(\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\,n\bmod2)\). Now \(n=2\lfloor n/2\rfloor+(n\bmod2)\) recovers the input, so the extended step is one-to-one. The extra bit records exactly the information the original step discarded, the last binary digit of \(n\).

exercises.question: Run Euclid’s algorithm on \((377,233)\). Count the divisions, record each quotient, and explain separately why the answer is correct and why the run stops.
hints: These are consecutive Fibonacci numbers.
exercises.answer: The remainders are \(144,89,55,34,21,13,8,5,3,2,1,0\): twelve divisions, with quotient \(1\) every time except the last, which is \(2\). The greatest common divisor is \(1\). It is correct because each step keeps the set of common divisors unchanged, an invariant. The run stops because the second entry strictly decreases through nonnegative integers. Quotients of \(1\) make that decrease as slow as possible.

exercises.question: Design a Turing machine that adds one to a binary number. The head starts on the rightmost digit, in state \(q\). Reading \(1\): write \(0\), move left, stay in \(q\). Reading \(0\) or a blank: write \(1\) and halt. Trace it on \(1011\) and on \(111\). How many steps does an \(n\)-digit input take in the worst case?
hints: Adding one turns trailing ones into zeros and the first zero into a one.
The worst case is an input of all ones.
exercises.answer: On \(1011\): read \(1\), write \(0\), move left (tape \(1010\)); read \(1\), write \(0\), move left (\(1000\)); read \(0\), write \(1\), halt (\(1100\)). Three steps, and \(1100\) is \(12=11+1\). On \(111\): three steps turn the ones into zeros, then the head reads the blank to the left, writes \(1\), and halts, giving \(1000\), which is \(8=7+1\), after four steps. In general the machine takes one step per trailing \(1\), plus one, so the worst case is \(n+1\) steps, for an input of all ones. The same finite rule table handles inputs of every length, which is the point of the model.

exercises.question: Euclid’s algorithm stops because the second entry decreases. Show something stronger: after any two steps, the second entry is less than half of what it was. Use this to bound the number of divisions for a pair \((a,b)\) with \(b\le233\), and compare with the run on \((377,233)\).
hints: From \((a,b)\) the next two pairs are \((b,r_1)\) and \((r_1,r_2)\). Consider separately \(r_1\le b/2\) and \(r_1>b/2\).
If \(r_1>b/2\), the division of \(b\) by \(r_1\) has quotient \(1\).
exercises.answer: If \(r_1\le b/2\), then \(r_2<r_1\le b/2\). If \(r_1>b/2\), then \(r_1\) goes into \(b\) once, so \(r_2=b-r_1<b/2\). Either way \(r_2<b/2\). So every two divisions at least halve the second entry. Starting from \(b\le233<2^8\), after \(16\) divisions the second entry is below \(233/2^8<1\), so it is \(0\): at most \(16\) divisions. The run on \((377,233)\) uses \(12\), close to this bound, because consecutive Fibonacci numbers have every quotient equal to \(1\), the slowest case. The bound grows with the number of digits of \(b\), not with \(b\) itself, a first example of measuring the resources an algorithm needs.

exercises.question: Show that no algorithm can decide, for every program \(P\) and input \(x\), whether \(P\) ever prints the word “hello” when run on \(x\). Use the undecidability of the halting problem: from a pair \((P,x)\), build a program \(P'\) that prints “hello” exactly when \(P\) halts on \(x\).
hints: \(P'\) should run \(P\) on \(x\) with all of \(P\)’s own output suppressed.
If a “hello” detector existed, what would it do on \(P'\)?
exercises.answer: Let \(P'\) simulate \(P\) on \(x\), discarding everything \(P\) would print, and print “hello” once the simulation halts. If \(P\) halts on \(x\), then \(P'\) prints “hello”. If not, the simulation runs forever and \(P'\) never prints anything. Building \(P'\) from \((P,x)\) is a mechanical rewriting of a finite description. Suppose an algorithm \(D\) decided whether a program prints “hello”. Then “build \(P'\), then run \(D\) on \(P'\)” would always finish and would answer whether \(P\) halts on \(x\). No such procedure exists, so \(D\) cannot exist. This pattern, turning a halting question into a question about another property, shows that many questions about program behavior are undecidable.

exercises.question: A student argues: “The halting problem is undecidable, so no algorithm can tell whether Euclid’s algorithm halts on \((48,18)\).” Explain what is wrong. Then describe an algorithm that answers correctly for one fixed program and input, and say why this does not contradict the theorem.
hints: The theorem is about one procedure that works for every pair.
For a single question with answer “yes” or “no,” one of two trivial programs answers correctly.
exercises.answer: The theorem excludes one algorithm that finishes with the correct answer for every program and input. It says nothing against settling particular cases. Euclid’s algorithm halts on \((48,18)\); we proved it halts on every pair of positive integers. More strikingly, every single question “does \(P\) halt on \(x\)?” is answered correctly by one of the two programs “print yes” and “print no.” One of them is right, even if we do not know which. Undecidability means that no single procedure, given \((P,x)\) as input, always finds the right answer. The difficulty lies in uniformity across all inputs, not in any one instance.

exercises.question: Make each step of Euclid’s algorithm reversible by recording its quotient. Show that \((b,r)\) and \(q\) determine the previous pair, and find how many quotients a run on \((377,233)\) must keep.
hints: The previous pair was \((a,b)\) with \(a=qb+r\).
Use the run from the worked problem.
exercises.answer: From \((b,r)\) and \(q\), the previous first entry is \(a=qb+r\), so the previous pair \((a,b)\) is recovered. A run that keeps all its quotients can be undone step by step. The run on \((377,233)\) keeps twelve quotients, eleven \(1\)s and one \(2\). Reversibility costs extra memory that grows with the length of the run.

exercises.question: Suppose, contrary to fact, that a halting decider \(H(P,x)\) existed. Show that it would turn proof search into a decision procedure for provability in a theory whose proofs can be checked mechanically: given a statement \(S\), build the program that searches for a proof of \(S\) and halts when it finds one. What would that imply for the incompleteness result of Section 1.3.3?
hints: The search program halts exactly when a proof of \(S\) exists.
With a decider for provability, try \(S\) and its negation.
exercises.answer: Let \(Q_S\) list candidate strings by length, check each, and halt on the first valid proof of \(S\). It halts exactly when \(S\) is provable. Running \(H(Q_S,\text{empty input})\) would always finish and report whether \(S\) is provable, so provability would be decidable. This is consistent with Section 1.1.3: the search alone may run forever, and \(H\) would supply the missing ability to recognize that it never ends. It would not remove incompleteness. Deciding whether \(S\) is provable is different from proving \(S\): with \(H\) we could recognize a sentence that is neither provable nor refutable, but it would remain unsettled by the axioms. The argument shows that provability is no harder to decide than halting, so the obstacle met in proof search is the same kind of obstacle the halting theorem identifies.

02-boolean-reversible-computation.purpose: Build computations from Boolean operations and learn how to preserve the information they would otherwise discard.
02-boolean-reversible-computation.before: Recall that a computation transforms configurations step by step, and that one function can have different implementations.
outcomes: Write a Boolean function as a truth table and as a polynomial modulo two.
Construct Boolean functions from NAND gates.
Verify a reversible function embedding.
Explain why temporary workspace is uncomputed rather than erased.
02-boolean-reversible-computation.limits: Logical reversibility alone does not guarantee low physical dissipation. Landauer’s bound concerns erasure under stated thermodynamic conditions.
02-boolean-reversible-computation.example: Follow a function value from a truth table to a reversible target update. The same update becomes the oracle in Chapter 7.
02-boolean-reversible-computation.next: Chapter 3 compares deterministic, nondeterministic, probabilistic, and quantum transitions on one example, and shows how quantum amplitudes make retained path information important.

exercises.question: Is the map \((x,y)\mapsto(x\lor y,\;x\land y)\) reversible?
hints: List the four outputs.
Look for two inputs with the same output.
exercises.answer: No. The inputs \(01\) and \(10\) both give \((1,0)\). Two output bits are not enough when the map merges inputs.

exercises.question: Write the binary-field polynomial of each function and check it on all four inputs: (a) \(\operatorname{NAND}(x,y)\); (b) the “equal” function, which is \(1\) exactly when \(x=y\).
hints: NAND is the negation of \(xy\), and negation adds \(1\).
“Equal” is the negation of XOR, which is \(x+y\).
exercises.answer: (a) \(\operatorname{NAND}(x,y)=1+xy\). On \(00,01,10\) the product is \(0\), giving \(1\); on \(11\) it gives \(1+1=0\). (b) “Equal” is \(1+x+y\): on \(00\) it is \(1\), on \(01\) and \(10\) it is \(1+1=0\), and on \(11\) it is \(1+1+1=1\). Both agree with the truth tables. Negating a function always means adding \(1\) modulo two, because \(1+0=1\) and \(1+1=0\).

exercises.question: Classical circuits copy bits freely by fan-out. Show that a CNOT whose target starts at \(0\) copies its control bit, and that the copying map \((a,0)\mapsto(a,a)\) is part of a reversible map. What does a Toffoli gate do to \((a,1,0)\)?
hints: CNOT sends \((a,b)\) to \((a,b\oplus a)\).
With one control fixed to \(1\), a Toffoli gate acts like a CNOT.
exercises.answer: CNOT gives \((a,0)\mapsto(a,0\oplus a)=(a,a)\): the target becomes a copy of the control. The full map \((a,b)\mapsto(a,b\oplus a)\) is reversible, since applying it twice restores both bits. Copying a bit is therefore reversible, provided the copy is written into a bit known to be \(0\). A Toffoli gate on \((a,1,0)\) gives \((a,1,0\oplus a\cdot1)=(a,1,a)\), another copy. Reversible fan-out costs a gate and a fresh bit, rather than being free. In quantum computation the same gate copies basis values, but it will not copy an unknown superposition, a distinction Chapter 6 develops.

exercises.question: Compute the three-bit majority function reversibly: using three Toffoli gates, turn \((x,y,z,t)\) into \((x,y,z,\,t\oplus\mathrm{maj}(x,y,z))\). Check the construction on the inputs \(110\) and \(100\) with \(t=0\).
hints: Majority is \(xy+yz+xz\) modulo two.
Each Toffoli gate adds one product to the target.
exercises.answer: Apply Toffoli gates with controls \((x,y)\), \((y,z)\), and \((x,z)\), each targeting \(t\). Together they add \(xy\oplus yz\oplus xz\), the polynomial of majority. On \(110\): \(1\oplus0\oplus0=1\). On \(100\): \(0\oplus0\oplus0=0\). The inputs are kept, so the map is reversible; it is its own inverse.

exercises.question: Find the binary-field polynomial of the three-bit function that is \(1\) exactly when exactly two of its inputs are \(1\). Build it from detectors, simplify, and check it on \(111\), \(110\), and \(100\). Compare it with the majority polynomial \(xy+yz+xz\).
hints: The rows with output \(1\) are \(011\), \(101\), and \(110\).
Expand each detector, such as \((1+x)yz=yz+xyz\), and collect terms modulo two.
exercises.answer: The detectors are \((1+x)yz=yz+xyz\), \(x(1+y)z=xz+xyz\), and \(xy(1+z)=xy+xyz\). Their sum is \(xy+yz+xz+3xyz=xy+yz+xz+xyz\) modulo two. On \(111\): \(1+1+1+1=0\), correct because three ones is not exactly two. On \(110\): \(1+0+0+0=1\), correct. On \(100\): all terms vanish, correct. The function differs from majority only on \(111\), where majority is \(1\), and the polynomials differ by exactly the term \(xyz\), the detector-like term that is \(1\) only on \(111\).

exercises.question: Convert the four-NAND XOR circuit of Section 2.2.2 into a reversible computation that leaves only the inputs and the answer. (a) How many Toffoli gates, CNOT gates, and extra bits does the compute–copy–uncompute construction use? (b) Trace every wire for \(a=1\), \(b=0\), and confirm that the workspace returns to its starting values.
hints: Each NAND becomes a Toffoli gate whose target starts at \(1\).
\(t=\operatorname{NAND}(a,b)\), \(u=\operatorname{NAND}(a,t)\), \(v=\operatorname{NAND}(b,t)\), output \(=\operatorname{NAND}(u,v)\).
exercises.answer: (a) Four Toffoli gates compute \(t,u,v\) and the XOR value into four bits that start at \(1\). One CNOT copies the answer into a fresh bit that starts at \(0\). Four more Toffoli gates, in reverse order, uncompute. That is eight Toffoli gates, one CNOT, and five extra bits. (b) For \(a=1,b=0\): \(t=\operatorname{NAND}(1,0)=1\), \(u=\operatorname{NAND}(1,1)=0\), \(v=\operatorname{NAND}(0,1)=1\), and the answer bit is \(\operatorname{NAND}(0,1)=1=1\oplus0\). The CNOT copies \(1\) into the fresh bit. Running the Toffoli gates backward restores the answer bit to \(1\), then \(v=1\oplus(0\cdot1)=1\), \(u=0\oplus(1\cdot1)=1\), and \(t=1\oplus(1\cdot0)=1\). All four workspace bits are back at \(1\), and only the inputs and the copied answer \(1\) remain.

exercises.question: A half adder adds two bits, producing a sum bit \(a\oplus b\) and a carry bit \(ab\). Build the reversible map \((a,b,0)\mapsto(a,\;a\oplus b,\;ab)\) from one Toffoli gate and one CNOT. Show that the order of the two gates matters by computing what the other order produces.
hints: The Toffoli gate needs the original \(b\) as a control.
If the CNOT acts first, the second bit holds \(a\oplus b\) when the Toffoli gate reads it.
exercises.answer: Apply the Toffoli gate with controls \(a,b\) and target the third bit: \((a,b,0)\to(a,b,ab)\). Then a CNOT from \(a\) to the second bit: \((a,b,ab)\to(a,a\oplus b,ab)\). Check: \(00\to(0,0,0)\), \(01\to(0,1,0)\), \(10\to(1,1,0)\), \(11\to(1,0,1)\), giving sum and carry correctly. In the other order, the CNOT first makes the second bit \(a\oplus b\), and the Toffoli gate then writes \(a(a\oplus b)=a(1+b)=a\land\lnot b\) into the third bit. On input \(11\) that gives carry \(0\), which is wrong. A reversible gate reads its controls at the moment it acts, so the order of gates is part of the circuit’s meaning.

exercises.question: A student says: “Uncomputation is just a roundabout way of erasing the workspace, so it must cost at least \(k_{\mathrm B}T\ln2\) per cleared bit.” In the three-bit AND example, explain why returning \(w=xy\) to \(0\) by a second Toffoli gate is not an erasure in Landauer’s sense, and what makes the difference.
hints: An erasure merges distinct states. Does the second Toffoli gate merge any two complete states?
While \(x\) and \(y\) are still present, is \(w\) uncertain?
exercises.answer: Landauer’s bound concerns maps that merge distinct states, such as a reset that sends both \(w=0\) and \(w=1\) to \(0\) without keeping the value elsewhere. The second Toffoli gate maps \((x,y,z,xy,xyz)\) to \((x,y,z,0,xyz)\), and as a map on all five bits it is one-to-one: it is its own inverse. It can clear \(w\) only because \(w\) is not independent information: it equals \(xy\), and \(x\) and \(y\) are still present. Uncomputation removes a redundant copy by undoing the step that made it, so nothing is lost. A reset would destroy the value of \(w\) even if \(x\) and \(y\) had already been discarded.

exercises.question: Build the reversible embedding of OR, \((x,y,t)\mapsto(x,y,t\oplus(x\lor y))\), from CNOT and Toffoli gates, and show that the circuit is its own inverse.
hints: \(x\lor y=x\oplus y\oplus xy\).
Each gate adds something to \(t\) and leaves \(x,y\) unchanged.
exercises.answer: CNOT from \(x\) to \(t\), CNOT from \(y\) to \(t\), and Toffoli from \((x,y)\) to \(t\) add \(x\oplus y\oplus xy=x\lor y\) to \(t\). Since none of the gates changes \(x\) or \(y\), running the circuit twice adds \(x\lor y\) twice, which cancels. The circuit is its own inverse, and with \(t=0\) it leaves the answer in \(t\).

exercises.question: A classical processor runs a computation \(10^9\) times per second, and each run leaves \(1000\) bits of intermediate values that are reset rather than uncomputed. (a) Using \(k_{\mathrm B}T\ln2\approx2.9\times10^{-21}\) J at \(300\) K, find the minimum power Landauer’s principle requires for these resets. (b) Compare it with a typical \(50\) W processor. (c) If the energy cost is so small, why does this course insist on uncomputation?
hints: Bits erased per second: \(10^9\times1000\).
Section 2.4.3 gives a reason that is not about energy.
exercises.answer: (a) \(10^{12}\) bits per second times \(2.9\times10^{-21}\) J is about \(2.9\times10^{-9}\) W, roughly three nanowatts. (b) That is about \(10^{10}\) times smaller than \(50\) W. Present-day processors dissipate far more than the Landauer bound for reasons unrelated to logical erasure: resistance, charging wires, and switching speed. (c) The reason for uncomputation here is not energy. In quantum computation, leftover intermediate values are records of the computation’s history, and such records prevent the interference that quantum algorithms rely on. Uncomputation is required for the computation to work at all, whatever it costs in heat.

03-amplitudes-interference.purpose: Understand why probabilities alone do not describe interference, and learn to calculate with amplitudes.
03-amplitudes-interference.before: Recall that a computation is a run of configurations, and that a reversible gate can be undone.
outcomes: Draw a transition rule as a state diagram, and list its runs as paths in a time-expanded diagram.
Apply the product rule along a path and the sum rule across paths.
Show why the same two-state probabilistic rule cannot reproduce two Hadamard steps.
Use the Born rule, and derive the constraints that preserve total probability.
Construct a complex square root of NOT.
Explain how a leftover record destroys interference and how uncomputation restores it.
03-amplitudes-interference.limits: The Born rule and unitary evolution are physical postulates. The examples motivate them; they do not derive quantum mechanics from classical probability. The next chapter explains the state after measurement.
03-amplitudes-interference.example: The same bit, updated twice, runs through the whole chapter. Its quantum version, two Hadamard steps, returns in Deutsch’s algorithm.
03-amplitudes-interference.next: Chapter 4 gives the amplitude rules a compact vector-and-matrix notation and adds measurement updates.

exercises.question: Two paths reach an outcome with amplitudes \(1/2\) and \(e^{i\pi/3}/2\). What is its probability?
hints: Add the amplitudes before squaring.
exercises.answer: \(|1+e^{i\pi/3}|^2/4=(2+2\cos60^\circ)/4=3/4\). Squaring each path first would give \(1/4+1/4=1/2\): the phases partly reinforce.

exercises.question: Which of these amplitude lists \((v_0,v_1)\) are normalized? (a) \((\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\); (b) \((\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2})\); (c) \((0.6,\,0.8i)\); (d) \((\tfrac{1+i}{2},\tfrac{1-i}{2})\). For each normalized list, give the two probabilities.
hints: Add the squared magnitudes \(|v_0|^2+|v_1|^2\).
exercises.answer: (a) \(\frac14+\frac14=\frac12\): not normalized, so these amplitudes cannot describe a state as they stand. (b) \(\frac12+\frac12=1\): normalized, probabilities \(\frac12,\frac12\). (c) \(0.36+0.64=1\): normalized, probabilities \(0.36\) and \(0.64\). (d) \(|1+i|^2/4=2/4=\frac12\) for each: normalized, probabilities \(\frac12,\frac12\). Signs and complex phases do not affect normalization; only magnitudes do.

exercises.question: Three states have amplitudes \(A=(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2})\), \(B=(-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2})\), and \(C=(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2})\). All give probabilities \(\frac12,\frac12\). Apply one Hadamard step to each. Which pairs remain indistinguishable, and why?
hints: \(B\) is \(A\) multiplied by \(-1\).
exercises.answer: \(A\) becomes \((1,0)\), so the result is \(0\) with certainty. \(B\) becomes \((-1,0)\), also \(0\) with certainty. \(C\) becomes \((0,1)\), so the result is \(1\) with certainty. \(A\) and \(B\) differ by a global phase \(-1\), which multiplies every later amplitude by the same factor and never changes a probability. \(A\) and \(C\) differ in relative phase, which the Hadamard step converts into a difference in outcome. Equal probabilities do not mean equal states.

exercises.question: An operation \(G\) on a qubit has the real weights \(\bra0G\ket0=\bra1G\ket1=\cos\alpha\), \(\bra1G\ket0=\sin\alpha\), and \(\bra0G\ket1=-\sin\alpha\). Check the two conditions on an operation, compute the two-step weights by path sums, and find the \(\alpha\) for which two steps send \(0\) to \(1\).
hints: The cross sum is \(\bra0G\ket0\bra0G\ket1+\bra1G\ket0\bra1G\ket1\).
Two steps from \(0\) give \(\cos2\alpha\) at \(0\) and \(\sin2\alpha\) at \(1\).
exercises.answer: The squares leaving each configuration add to \(\cos^2\alpha+\sin^2\alpha=1\), and the cross sum is \(-\cos\alpha\sin\alpha+\sin\alpha\cos\alpha=0\). From \(0\): weight \(\cos^2\alpha-\sin^2\alpha=\cos2\alpha\) at \(0\) and \(2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha=\sin2\alpha\) at \(1\). From \(1\): \(-\sin2\alpha\) at \(0\) and \(\cos2\alpha\) at \(1\). At \(\alpha=\pi/4\), two steps send \(0\) to \(1\) and \(1\) to \(-0\): NOT, except for a relative sign. Real weights reach NOT only up to this sign; exactly NOT needs complex weights.

exercises.question: A proposed step \(S\) has all four weights \(\bra jS\ket i\) equal to \(1/\sqrt2\). (a) Check the outgoing-normalization condition for each definite input. (b) Check the cross-sum condition \(\sum_j(\bra jS\ket0)^*\bra jS\ket1=0\). (c) Apply the step to the normalized input \((\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2})\) and find the total of the squared magnitudes. What goes wrong?
hints: From either input the outgoing squared magnitudes are \(\frac12+\frac12\).
Each new amplitude is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(v_0+v_1)\).
exercises.answer: (a) From \(0\) or from \(1\) the outgoing squared magnitudes are \(\frac12+\frac12=1\), so definite inputs stay normalized. (b) The cross sum is \(\frac12+\frac12=1\neq0\), so the condition fails. (c) Each new amplitude is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big)=1\), so the output is \((1,1)\), with total \(2\). The “probabilities” would add to \(2\). Because contributions from the two inputs always reinforce, the cross terms add instead of cancelling. The Hadamard step avoids this with its single negative weight, which makes the cross sum \(\frac12-\frac12=0\). Checking definite inputs alone is not enough.

exercises.question: Let \(\sqrt X\) be the square root of NOT, with stay-weight \(a=(1+i)/2\) and switch-weight \(b=(1-i)/2\). Starting at \(\ket0\), find the amplitudes after three steps of \(\sqrt X\), and after four. Use \(\sqrt X\sqrt X=X\) to shorten the calculation, and give the probabilities.
hints: Three steps are two steps (\(X\)) followed by one more, or one followed by two.
One step from \(0\) gives \((a,b)\); NOT exchanges the two amplitudes.
exercises.answer: One step from \(0\) gives amplitudes \((a,b)=\big(\frac{1+i}{2},\frac{1-i}{2}\big)\). Two steps give NOT, so three steps are one step followed by NOT, which exchanges the amplitudes: \(\big(\frac{1-i}{2},\frac{1+i}{2}\big)\). Each has squared magnitude \(\frac12\), so the probabilities are \(\frac12,\frac12\). Four steps are NOT twice, which does nothing: the amplitudes are \((1,0)\), and the run returns to \(0\) with certainty. After one or three steps the outcome looks like a fair coin, yet the next steps can still produce a certain result. The amplitudes retain information that the probabilities do not show.

exercises.question: Repeat the path-information experiment of Section 3.4.3 with a different “record”: between the two Hadamard steps on the first label, apply NOT to the record bit whatever the first label is. Track the four amplitudes from \(00\) and find the final probabilities. Does the first label still return to \(0\) with certainty? Explain using complete configurations.
hints: After the first \(H\), the occupied configurations are \(00\) and \(10\); NOT on the record turns them into \(01\) and \(11\).
Both paths now carry the same record value.
exercises.answer: After the first \(H\): \(00\) and \(10\), each with amplitude \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\). NOT on the record gives \(01\) and \(11\). The final \(H\) on the first label sends \(01\) to \(01\) and \(11\) with weights \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\), and \(11\) to \(01\) with \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\) and to \(11\) with \(-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\). The totals are \(\frac12+\frac12=1\) at \(01\) and \(\frac12-\frac12=0\) at \(11\). So the outcome is \(01\) with certainty: the first label returns to \(0\), and the record reads \(1\). The record changed, but identically on both paths, so the two paths still meet at the same complete configurations and interfere. Only a record that distinguishes the paths prevents interference.

exercises.question: A student says: “After one Hadamard step from \(0\), the bit is \(0\) or \(1\) with probability \(\frac12\) each. That is the same as a fair coin, so a second Hadamard step should act like a second coin flip, giving \(\frac12,\frac12\) again.” Compute what actually happens, and identify the step in the student’s reasoning that fails.
hints: Add the amplitudes of the two paths to each endpoint before squaring.
Would a fair coin have the same amplitudes, or only the same probabilities?
exercises.answer: Two Hadamard steps from \(0\) give amplitude \(\frac12+\frac12=1\) at \(0\) and \(\frac12-\frac12=0\) at \(1\): the result is \(0\) with certainty. The student treated the intermediate state as a probability distribution and combined the two paths by adding probabilities, \(\frac14+\frac14\). But the intermediate state is the amplitude list \((\frac{1}{\sqrt2},\frac{1}{\sqrt2})\), and the paths to each endpoint must be combined by adding amplitudes, which can cancel. Equal probabilities after one step do not determine what happens after the next. The amplitudes carry the signs that make cancellation possible, and a coin’s probabilities do not.

exercises.question: Apply \(H\), then the phase step \(R\) with \(\bra0R\ket0=1\) and \(\bra1R\ket1=e^{i\phi}\), then \(H\), to \(0\). Using path sums, find the probability of outcome \(0\) as a function of \(\phi\), and the values of \(\phi\) that make each outcome certain.
hints: There are two paths to each final configuration.
The path through \(1\) picks up the factor \(e^{i\phi}\).
exercises.answer: To \(0\): \(\tfrac12+\tfrac12e^{i\phi}\). To \(1\): \(\tfrac12-\tfrac12e^{i\phi}\). The probability of \(0\) is \(|1+e^{i\phi}|^2/4=(1+\cos\phi)/2\). Outcome \(0\) is certain at \(\phi=0\) and outcome \(1\) at \(\phi=\pi\). A phase that no direct measurement sees controls the result completely.

exercises.question: Find a one-bit step \(A\) that changes only phases (\(\bra1A\ket0=\bra0A\ket1=0\)) and satisfies \(A^2=Z\). How many such steps are there? Then compute the probability of \(0\) after \(H\), \(A\), \(H\) starting at \(0\), and compare it with \(H\), \(Z\), \(H\). What does “half of \(Z\)” do to the interference?
hints: Write \(\bra0A\ket0=p\), \(\bra1A\ket1=q\), and require \(p^2=1\), \(q^2=-1\).
Use \(p(0)=(1+\cos\phi)/2\) for a relative phase \(\phi\).
exercises.answer: Two steps of a diagonal step multiply each weight by itself, so \(p^2=1\) and \(q^2=-1\): \(p=\pm1\) and \(q=\pm i\). That gives four steps, and each satisfies normalization because \(|p|=|q|=1\). Take \(A\) with \(p=1\), \(q=i\). After \(H\) the amplitudes are \((\frac{1}{\sqrt2},\frac{1}{\sqrt2})\); \(A\) changes them to \((\frac{1}{\sqrt2},\frac{i}{\sqrt2})\), a relative phase \(\pi/2\). The final \(H\) gives \(p(0)=(1+\cos\frac\pi2)/2=\frac12\). With \(Z\), the relative phase is \(\pi\) and \(p(0)=0\); with no step it is \(0\) and \(p(0)=1\). Half the phase gives a probability halfway between, not a step halfway between “keep” and “flip.” The step with \(q=i\) reappears in later chapters as the phase gate \(S\).

04-states-measurement.purpose: Use state vectors and inner products to describe transition amplitudes and geometry, then express operations as matrices and calculate measurement outcomes.
04-states-measurement.before: The prerequisites are the ket notation for states and arrow weights, complex amplitudes, normalization, path sums, the cross-sum condition, and complete configuration labels developed in Chapter 3. This chapter turns kets into vectors and steps into matrices, and adds the state update after measurement.
outcomes: Write states as vectors and interpret inner products as final-state amplitudes.
Represent operations as matrices and use adjoints to test unitarity.
Compute projective measurement probabilities and conditional states in the computational and rotated bases.
Explain how tensor products describe composite systems and allow entangled pure states.
04-states-measurement.limits: The main text treats finite-dimensional pure states and projective measurements. Mixed states and general measurements are in Appendix D.
04-states-measurement.example: Compare state vectors by their inner products, then predict how the same preparation responds to Z and X measurements and follow the conditional state update.
04-states-measurement.next: Chapter 5 combines these postulates into the quantum circuit model of computation.

exercises.question: For \(\ket\psi=\tfrac35\ket0+\tfrac45\ket1\), compute the amplitudes \(\braket{+}{\psi}\) and \(\braket{-}{\psi}\), where \(\ket\pm=(\ket0\pm\ket1)/\sqrt2\). Find the two probabilities and check that they add to one. Why must they?
hints: \(\braket{\pm}{\psi}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\psi_0\pm\psi_1)\) for real coordinates.
\(\ket+\) and \(\ket-\) form an orthonormal basis.
exercises.answer: \(\braket{+}{\psi}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(\frac35+\frac45\big)=\frac{7}{5\sqrt2}\), with probability \(\frac{49}{50}\). \(\braket{-}{\psi}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(\frac35-\frac45\big)=-\frac{1}{5\sqrt2}\), with probability \(\frac{1}{50}\). They add to \(1\). The vectors \(\ket+\) and \(\ket-\) are orthonormal, so \(\ket\psi=\braket{+}{\psi}\ket++\braket{-}{\psi}\ket-\) and its squared length, \(1\), is the sum of the two squared components. In the computational basis the same state gives \(\frac{9}{25}\) and \(\frac{16}{25}\): different tests, different probabilities, one state.

exercises.question: Is \(U=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\i&-i\end{pmatrix}\) unitary? Check that its columns have unit length and are orthogonal, then compute \(U\ket0\) and \(U\ket1\).
hints: Column \(0\) is \((1,i)/\sqrt2\) and column \(1\) is \((1,-i)/\sqrt2\).
Conjugate the first column’s entries when computing the overlap.
exercises.answer: Each column has squared length \(\frac12(1+1)=1\). Their overlap is \(\frac12\big(1^*\cdot1+i^*\cdot(-i)\big)=\frac12\big(1+(-i)(-i)\big)=\frac12(1-1)=0\). So the columns are orthonormal and \(U\) is unitary. The columns are the images: \(U\ket0=(\ket0+i\ket1)/\sqrt2\) and \(U\ket1=(\ket0-i\ket1)/\sqrt2\). These are two orthogonal states with equal computational-basis probabilities; they differ only in relative phase.

exercises.question: Which pairs describe the same physical state? (a) \((\ket0+i\ket1)/\sqrt2\) and \((i\ket0-\ket1)/\sqrt2\); (b) \((\ket0+i\ket1)/\sqrt2\) and \((\ket0-i\ket1)/\sqrt2\); (c) \(\ket1\) and \(-\ket1\). For the pair that differs, compute the inner product.
hints: Look for a single factor \(e^{i\gamma}\) that converts one vector into the other.
Conjugate the left vector’s coordinates in the inner product.
exercises.answer: (a) Same: \(i(\ket0+i\ket1)=i\ket0-\ket1\), a global phase \(i\). (c) Same: a global phase \(-1\). (b) Different: no common factor works, because the first coordinates would require the factor \(1\) and the second would then require \(i=-i\). Their inner product is \(\frac12\big(1\cdot1+(-i)(-i)\big)=\frac12(1-1)=0\), so they are orthogonal: a test along one direction never reports the other. A relative phase can make two states with identical computational-basis probabilities perfectly distinguishable.

exercises.question: Let \(U=\frac15\begin{pmatrix}4&-3\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\). Starting from \(\ket0\): (a) apply \(U\) twice and then measure, giving both probabilities; (b) apply \(U\), measure, apply \(U\), and measure, giving the probability that the final outcome is \(0\). Explain the difference.
hints: \(U^2=\frac{1}{25}\begin{pmatrix}7&-24\\24&7\end{pmatrix}\).
In (b), sum over the two possible intermediate outcomes, each followed by \(U\) from a definite state.
exercises.answer: (a) \(U^2\ket0=\frac{1}{25}(7\ket0+24\ket1)\), so outcome \(0\) has probability \(\frac{49}{625}\approx0.078\) and outcome \(1\) has \(\frac{576}{625}\approx0.922\). (b) After the first \(U\), the measurement gives \(0\) with probability \(\frac{16}{25}\) and \(1\) with \(\frac{9}{25}\), leaving \(\ket0\) or \(\ket1\). From \(\ket0\), \(U\) gives outcome \(0\) with probability \(\frac{16}{25}\); from \(\ket1\), with probability \(\frac{9}{25}\). So \(p(0)=\frac{16}{25}\cdot\frac{16}{25}+\frac{9}{25}\cdot\frac{9}{25}=\frac{337}{625}\approx0.539\). Without the measurement, the two routes to \(0\) have amplitudes \(\frac{16}{25}\) and \(-\frac{9}{25}\), which partly cancel. The intermediate measurement keeps one route per run, so probabilities add instead of amplitudes.

exercises.question: For \(U=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\i&-i\end{pmatrix}\), compute \(U^\dagger\) and verify \(U^\dagger U=I\). Then use the adjoint to find the state \(\ket\psi\) with \(U\ket\psi=\ket0\), and check your answer by applying \(U\).
hints: \((U^\dagger)_{ij}=U_{ji}^*\): transpose and conjugate.
If \(U\ket\psi=\ket0\), then \(\ket\psi=U^\dagger\ket0\).
exercises.answer: Transposing and conjugating gives \(U^\dagger=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\\1&i\end{pmatrix}\). Then \(U^\dagger U=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1+(-i)(i)&1+(-i)(-i)\\1+i\cdot i&1+i(-i)\end{pmatrix}=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}=I\). Since \(U\) is unitary, \(U^\dagger\) undoes it: \(\ket\psi=U^\dagger\ket0=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0+\ket1)\), the first column of \(U^\dagger\). Check: \(U\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0+\ket1)=\frac12\big((1+1)\ket0+(i-i)\ket1\big)=\ket0\). The adjoint gives the inverse without solving equations, but only because \(U\) is unitary.

exercises.question: Write \(\ket\psi=\tfrac12\ket0+\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}e^{i\pi/3}\ket1\) in the form \(\cos\frac\theta2\ket0+e^{i\phi}\sin\frac\theta2\ket1\). Then find the state of the same form that is orthogonal to it, and check the orthogonality. What happens to \(\theta\) and \(\phi\) when \(Z\) is applied to \(\ket\psi\)?
hints: \(\cos\frac\theta2=\frac12\) gives \(\theta\).
Try \(\sin\frac\theta2\ket0-e^{i\phi}\cos\frac\theta2\ket1\) for the orthogonal state.
exercises.answer: \(\cos\frac\theta2=\frac12\) gives \(\theta=\frac{2\pi}{3}\), and then \(\sin\frac\theta2=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\) and \(\phi=\frac\pi3\). Take \(\ket{\psi^\perp}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\ket0-e^{i\pi/3}\frac12\ket1\). Then \(\braket{\psi^\perp}{\psi}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac12+\big(-e^{-i\pi/3}\tfrac12\big)\big(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}e^{i\pi/3}\big)=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}-\frac{\sqrt3}{4}=0\). In the standard form, \(\ket{\psi^\perp}\) has \(\theta'=\pi-\theta=\frac\pi3\) and \(\phi'=\phi+\pi\). Applying \(Z\) multiplies the \(\ket1\) amplitude by \(-1=e^{i\pi}\): \(\theta\) stays \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\) and \(\phi\) becomes \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\). \(Z\) changes only the relative phase, so computational-basis probabilities are unchanged.

exercises.question: Show that a two-qubit state \(\sum_{ij}c_{ij}\ket{ij}\) is a product state only if \(c_{00}c_{11}=c_{01}c_{10}\). Apply the test to (a) \(\frac12(\ket{00}+\ket{01}+\ket{10}-\ket{11})\); (b) \(\frac12(\ket{00}+i\ket{01}+\ket{10}+i\ket{11})\). For the product state, find the factors.
hints: For a product, \(c_{ij}=a_ib_j\), so both sides equal \(a_0a_1b_0b_1\).
In (b), try factoring out \(\ket0+\ket1\) on the first qubit.
exercises.answer: If \(c_{ij}=a_ib_j\), then \(c_{00}c_{11}=a_0b_0a_1b_1=c_{01}c_{10}\). (a) \(c_{00}c_{11}=-\frac14\) but \(c_{01}c_{10}=\frac14\): the test fails, so the state is entangled, even though every computational-basis outcome has probability \(\frac14\). (b) \(c_{00}c_{11}=\frac i4=c_{01}c_{10}\), and indeed the state is \(\frac{\ket0+\ket1}{\sqrt2}\otimes\frac{\ket0+i\ket1}{\sqrt2}\). Expanding the product reproduces all four amplitudes. Uniform probabilities do not reveal whether a state is entangled; the relations among the amplitudes do. (The converse also holds: when the condition is met, the state factors.)

exercises.question: A student says: “The state \((\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2\) means the qubit is really \(0\) or really \(1\), each with probability \(\frac12\); we just don’t know which.” Propose an experiment that distinguishes the superposition from a qubit prepared as \(\ket0\) or \(\ket1\) by a fair coin, and compute its predictions for both.
hints: Apply \(H\) before measuring.
For the coin preparation, average the results for \(\ket0\) and \(\ket1\).
exercises.answer: Apply \(H\) and then measure in the computational basis. The superposition gives \(H\frac{\ket0+\ket1}{\sqrt2}=\ket0\): outcome \(0\) with certainty. For the coin preparation, \(H\ket0\) and \(H\ket1\) each give outcome \(0\) with probability \(\frac12\), so the average is \(\frac12\). A computational-basis measurement alone cannot tell the two preparations apart, but the Hadamard step reveals the difference, because the superposition has a definite relative phase between its amplitudes and the coin preparation has none. A superposition is a definite state, not a description of our ignorance.

exercises.question: Prove that a unitary preserves inner products: \(\braket{U\phi}{U\psi}=\braket\phi\psi\). Deduce that no unitary can map \(\ket0\) and \(\ket+\) to two orthogonal states. Explain why this means that no measurement, even after any closed-system evolution, distinguishes \(\ket0\) from \(\ket+\) with certainty.
hints: Use \(\braket{U\phi}{U\psi}=\bra\phi U^\dagger U\ket\psi\).
\(\braket0+=1/\sqrt2\).
exercises.answer: By the defining property of the adjoint, \(\braket{U\phi}{U\psi}=\bra\phi U^\dagger U\ket\psi=\braket\phi\psi\), since \(U^\dagger U=I\). For \(\ket0\) and \(\ket+\), the overlap is \(1/\sqrt2\), and so is the overlap of \(U\ket0\) and \(U\ket+\) for every unitary \(U\): the images are never orthogonal. A computational-basis measurement that always gave one outcome for the first state and the other outcome for the second would require the two evolved states to lie along different basis directions, which are orthogonal. So no sequence of unitary steps followed by such a measurement separates \(\ket0\) from \(\ket+\) perfectly. Nonorthogonal states can be told apart only with some probability of error, a limit that Quantum Information develops in detail.

exercises.question: Count the real parameters needed to specify (a) a general pure state of \(n\) qubits and (b) a product of \(n\) one-qubit pure states, after removing normalization and global phase. Evaluate both for \(n=2\) and \(n=10\). What does the comparison suggest about how common entangled states are?
hints: A general state has \(2^n\) complex amplitudes; normalization and global phase remove two real parameters.
Each qubit in a product needs two real parameters, \(\theta\) and \(\phi\).
exercises.answer: (a) \(2^n\) complex amplitudes are \(2\cdot2^n\) real numbers. Normalization removes one and global phase another, leaving \(2^{n+1}-2\). (b) Each qubit needs \(\theta\) and \(\phi\), so a product needs \(2n\). For \(n=2\): \(6\) against \(4\). For \(n=10\): \(2046\) against \(20\). Product states form a thin subset of all pure states, and the gap grows exponentially. A randomly chosen pure state of many qubits is therefore almost never a product. This is also why a classical description of a general \(n\)-qubit state needs exponentially many numbers, while a product state needs only \(2n\).

06-composite-systems.purpose: Extend the single-qubit model to computations on joint registers, including measurement and classical control.
06-composite-systems.before: Use the state and composition rules of Chapter 4 and the single-qubit circuits of Chapter 5.
outcomes: Track joint amplitudes through local and controlled gates.
Calculate joint, marginal, and conditional measurement probabilities.
Distinguish entanglement from classical correlation and explain the limits on copying and signalling.
Follow teleportation through all four outcomes and corrections.
Explain what one parallel evaluation of a function produces, and why a measurement reveals only one input–value pair.
06-composite-systems.limits: Teleportation transfers a state using shared entanglement and classical communication; it does not transmit a controllable signal faster than light.
06-composite-systems.example: Compute a two-qubit circuit, prepare and test a Bell state, use a shared pair in teleportation, then evaluate AND on all four inputs at once.
06-composite-systems.next: Chapter 7 asks which global property of a function interference can extract, and prepares the target so that it keeps no record of the branch.

exercises.question: Is \((\ket{00}+\ket{01}+\ket{10})/\sqrt3\) entangled?
hints: A product state satisfies \(\alpha_{00}\alpha_{11}=\alpha_{01}\alpha_{10}\).
Here \(\alpha_{11}=0\).
exercises.answer: \(\alpha_{00}\alpha_{11}=0\) but \(\alpha_{01}\alpha_{10}=1/3\), so the state is not a product: it is entangled.

exercises.question: Two qubits are prepared independently: the first in \((\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2\), the second in \(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\ket0+\frac12\ket1\). Write the four joint amplitudes, the probability that the two measured bits agree, and the marginal probability that the second bit is \(0\).
hints: Joint amplitudes are products of local amplitudes.
“Agree” means the outcomes \(00\) or \(11\).
exercises.answer: The amplitudes are \(\frac{\sqrt3}{2\sqrt2}\), \(\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}\), \(\frac{\sqrt3}{2\sqrt2}\), \(\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}\) for \(00,01,10,11\), with probabilities \(\frac38,\frac18,\frac38,\frac18\). The bits agree with probability \(\frac38+\frac18=\frac12\). The second bit is \(0\) with probability \(\frac38+\frac38=\frac34\), exactly its local probability: for a product state the marginals are the single-qubit probabilities, and the joint probabilities factor.

exercises.question: Alice holds the first qubit of \(\ket{\Phi^+}=(\ket{00}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2\). Find the joint state after she applies (a) \(Z\), (b) \(X\), (c) \(Z\) and then \(X\). Does any of these change Bob’s computational-basis probabilities?
hints: Apply the gate to the first label of each term.
Bob’s probability of \(b\) is the sum of \(|\alpha_{ab}|^2\) over \(a\).
exercises.answer: (a) \(Z\) gives \((\ket{00}-\ket{11})/\sqrt2\). (b) \(X\) gives \((\ket{10}+\ket{01})/\sqrt2\). (c) \(Z\) then \(X\) gives \((\ket{10}-\ket{01})/\sqrt2\). Together with \(\ket{\Phi^+}\) these are four orthogonal states, so a local gate by Alice changes the joint state in a way a joint measurement could detect. Bob’s computational-basis probabilities stay \(\frac12,\frac12\) in every case, as no-signalling requires: the change is visible only by comparing both qubits.

exercises.question: Prepare \((\ket{01}-\ket{10})/\sqrt2\) from \(\ket{00}\) using X, H, and CNOT. Calculate the outcomes if H is then applied to both qubits before measurement.
hints: Prepare 11 first, then use H on the first qubit followed by CNOT.
Expand the two contributions separately before adding.
exercises.answer: X on both wires gives 11. H on the first gives \((\ket{01}-\ket{11})/\sqrt2\), and CNOT gives \((\ket{01}-\ket{10})/\sqrt2\). Applying H on both sends this to \((\ket{10}-\ket{01})/\sqrt2\), differing only by a global minus sign. Outcomes 01 and 10 each occur with probability one half.

exercises.question: Measure the first qubit of \(\ket\Psi=\frac12(\ket{00}+\ket{01}+\ket{10}+i\ket{11})\). Give each outcome probability and the conditional state of the second qubit. Is \(\ket\Psi\) entangled? Then, for each first outcome, find the probability that a \(\pm\)-basis measurement of the second qubit (apply \(H\), then measure) gives \(0\).
hints: Keep the terms with the observed first label and renormalize.
\(H\) maps \((\ket0+e^{i\phi}\ket1)/\sqrt2\) to amplitude \((1+e^{i\phi})/2\) on \(\ket0\).
exercises.answer: Each first outcome has probability \(\frac14+\frac14=\frac12\). After outcome \(0\) the second qubit is \((\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2\); after outcome \(1\) it is \((\ket0+i\ket1)/\sqrt2\). The conditional state depends on the outcome, so \(\ket\Psi\) is entangled; consistently, \(\alpha_{00}\alpha_{11}=\frac i4\neq\frac14=\alpha_{01}\alpha_{10}\). In the \(\pm\) test, the first conditional state gives \(0\) with probability \(1\); the second gives \(|(1+i)/2|^2=\frac12\). The computational-basis statistics of the second qubit are the same for both outcomes, \(\frac12,\frac12\). The entanglement shows up only in a measurement sensitive to relative phase.

exercises.question: Prepare three qubits from \(\ket{000}\) with \(H\) on the first qubit, CNOT from the first to the second, and CNOT from the second to the third. (a) Track the state. (b) Apply \(H\) to all three qubits and find which outcomes occur and with what probabilities. (c) Compare with a classical mixture of \(000\) and \(111\) prepared by a fair coin.
hints: \(H^{\otimes3}\ket{000}\) has all eight amplitudes \(+\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}\); \(H^{\otimes3}\ket{111}\) has sign \((-1)^{z_1+z_2+z_3}\) on \(\ket z\).
Add the two contributions to each outcome.
exercises.answer: (a) \(\ket{000}\to\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{000}+\ket{100})\to\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{000}+\ket{110})\to\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{000}+\ket{111})\). (b) The amplitude of outcome \(z\) is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}\big(1+(-1)^{z_1+z_2+z_3}\big)\). It is \(\frac12\) when \(z\) has an even number of ones and \(0\) otherwise. So the four outcomes \(000,011,101,110\) each occur with probability \(\frac14\), and the outcomes with odd parity never occur. (c) For the mixture, each preparation gives all eight outcomes with probability \(\frac18\), and so does their average. In the computational basis the two preparations look identical, but after the Hadamards the coherent state shows a strict parity rule that the mixture lacks.

exercises.question: CNOT copies \(\ket0\) and \(\ket1\) into a blank target. Use it on \(\ket+\ket0\) and test the result as if it were two copies of \(\ket+\): apply \(H\) to both qubits and measure. What fraction of runs pass the test (outcome \(00\)), and what fraction would pass for genuine copies \(\ket+\ket+\)?
hints: CNOT turns \(\ket+\ket0\) into \(\ket{\Phi^+}\).
\((H\otimes H)\ket{\Phi^+}=\ket{\Phi^+}\).
exercises.answer: CNOT gives \((\ket{00}+\ket{11})/\sqrt2=\ket{\Phi^+}\). Applying \(H\otimes H\) returns \(\ket{\Phi^+}\) (Section 6.2.3), so the measurement gives \(00\) or \(11\), each with probability \(\frac12\). The test passes in half the runs. Genuine copies \(\ket+\ket+\) become \(\ket{00}\) and would pass every time. CNOT is a perfect copier for the basis states and fails for \(\ket+\): it produces an entangled pair, not two independent copies. No-cloning says this failure is unavoidable for any single device that copies both \(\ket0\) and \(\ket+\).

exercises.question: A student reasons: “Each qubit of \(\ket{\Phi^+}\) gives \(0\) or \(1\) with probability \(\frac12\), so each qubit by itself is in the state \(\ket+\).” Test this by computing the probability that the first qubit alone gives \(0\) in the \(\pm\) basis (apply \(H\) to it, then measure). What would \(\ket+\) predict? Can any single-qubit pure state reproduce the first qubit’s statistics?
hints: \((H\otimes I)\ket{\Phi^+}=\frac12(\ket{00}+\ket{10}+\ket{01}-\ket{11})\).
For any pure state there is a measurement, after a suitable gate, with a certain outcome.
exercises.answer: \((H\otimes I)\ket{\Phi^+}=\frac12(\ket{00}+\ket{10}+\ket{01}-\ket{11})\), so the first qubit gives \(0\) with probability \(\frac14+\frac14=\frac12\). The state \(\ket+\) would give \(0\) with certainty. The first qubit gives \(\frac12,\frac12\) in both the computational and the \(\pm\) basis, and the same holds for every other test. A pure state \(\ket\psi\) always has a test with a certain result, namely the one that checks for \(\ket\psi\) itself. So no pure state describes half of a Bell pair: its statistics match a fair coin in every basis. The precise description of such a part needs the mixed-state tools of Appendix D.

exercises.question: Teleport \(\ket\psi=(\ket0+i\ket1)/\sqrt2\). For each of Alice’s four outcomes \((m,n)\), give Bob’s state before correction and the correction he applies.
hints: Bob holds \(X^nZ^m\ket\psi\).
He applies \(X^n\), then \(Z^m\).
exercises.answer: \((0,0)\): \((\ket0+i\ket1)/\sqrt2\), no correction. \((0,1)\): \((i\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2\), apply \(X\). \((1,0)\): \((\ket0-i\ket1)/\sqrt2\), apply \(Z\). \((1,1)\): \((-i\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2\), apply \(X\) and then \(Z\). In every case the result is \(\ket\psi\).

exercises.question: Repeat the parallel evaluation of Section 6.5 with the target prepared in \(\ket-=(\ket0-\ket1)/\sqrt2\) instead of \(\ket0\). (a) Show that \(U_f\ket x\ket-=(-1)^{f(x)}\ket x\ket-\). (b) Apply \(H\otimes H\) to the inputs and compute \(p(00)\) for a constant \(f\), for \(f(x)=x_1\), and for AND. (c) Why does the target \(\ket-\) succeed where \(\ket0\) failed?
hints: \(U_f\) either leaves \(\ket-\) alone or flips it, and \(X\ket-=-\ket-\).
The amplitude of readout \(00\) is \(\frac14\sum_x(-1)^{f(x)}\).
exercises.answer: (a) If \(f(x)=0\), the target is untouched. If \(f(x)=1\), it is flipped, and \(\frac{\ket1-\ket0}{\sqrt2}=-\ket-\). So \(U_f\ket x\ket-=(-1)^{f(x)}\ket x\ket-\). (b) Starting from the uniform input superposition, the state after \(U_f\) is \(\frac12\sum_x(-1)^{f(x)}\ket x\otimes\ket-\), and the readout \(00\) has amplitude \(\frac14\sum_x(-1)^{f(x)}\). Constant \(f\): \(\pm1\), so \(p(00)=1\). \(f(x)=x_1\): two \(+1\) and two \(-1\), so \(p(00)=0\). AND: \(\frac14(3-1)=\frac12\), so \(p(00)=\frac14\). (c) The target ends in \(\ket-\) on every branch, so it keeps no record of the input. The function values move into signs on the input branches, and those signs can reinforce or cancel at the common readout. Chapter 7 develops this effect, phase kickback.

07-queries-phase-kickback.purpose: Use a reversible query to encode a property in relative phase and read it through interference.
07-queries-phase-kickback.before: Use reversible target updates, the Hadamard transformation, and joint-state notation.
outcomes: Derive phase kickback using \(\ket-\).
Calculate the output of Deutsch’s algorithm.
State exactly what a query advantage counts.
07-queries-phase-kickback.limits: Deutsch’s task here uses a one-bit Boolean function and an ideal reversible oracle. A single query does not reveal every function value.
07-queries-phase-kickback.example: The reversible target update of a function becomes a phase mark, and two-path interference becomes the readout.
07-queries-phase-kickback.next: Chapter 8 constructs the oracle and other operations from elementary gates.

exercises.question: For \(f=(0,1)\), what does \(U_f\) do to \(\ket1\ket-\)?
hints: \(f(1)=1\), so the target flips.
exercises.answer: The target flips, which multiplies \(\ket-\) by \(-1\): \(U_f\ket1\ket-=-\ket1\ket-\). The function value appears as a sign, and the target is unchanged.

exercises.question: A programmer prepares the target of Deutsch’s algorithm as \(\ket1\) but forgets the Hadamard on it, so the query acts on \(\ket+\ket1\). For the balanced function \(f=(0,1)\), find the state after the query and the probability that the final input measurement gives the correct answer \(1\).
hints: \(U_f\ket x\ket1=\ket x\ket{1\oplus f(x)}\).
Do the two input branches end with the same target label?
exercises.answer: The query gives \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0\ket1+\ket1\ket0)\): the target now records the input branch, exactly as with a blank target. After \(H\) on the input, the state is \(\frac12(\ket0\ket1+\ket1\ket1+\ket0\ket0-\ket1\ket0)\), and the input reads \(1\) with probability \(\frac14+\frac14=\frac12\). The target \(\ket1\) is a basis state, not an eigenstate of the flip, so the function value is written into the target instead of being kicked back as a sign. Only \(\ket-\) works.

exercises.question: For \(n=3\) input bits under the constant-or-balanced promise, how many queries does an exact deterministic classical algorithm need in the worst case? A randomized algorithm queries \(k\) inputs chosen uniformly at random (with replacement) and answers “constant” if all values agree. With what probability can it be wrong on a balanced function, and how large must \(k\) be for an error below \(1\%\)?
hints: The worst case for a deterministic algorithm sees half the inputs agree.
On a balanced function, all \(k\) values agree with probability \(2\cdot2^{-k}\).
exercises.answer: Deterministically, \(2^{n-1}+1=5\) queries are needed: after \(4\) equal answers the function could still be balanced. The randomized algorithm is never wrong on a constant function. On a balanced one, each query returns \(0\) or \(1\) with probability \(\frac12\), and all \(k\) agree with probability \(2^{1-k}\). That is below \(0.01\) for \(k\ge8\). Deutsch–Jozsa uses one query and never errs, but against algorithms allowed a small error the classical cost stays constant as \(n\) grows. The size of a quantum advantage depends on which classical success criterion is used for comparison.

exercises.question: Run the \(n\)-qubit version of Deutsch’s algorithm for \(n=2\) and the balanced function \(f(x_1x_2)=x_1\). Show that the outcome \(00\) never occurs.
hints: After the query the input amplitudes are \((-1)^{x_1}/2\).
Factor the input state before applying \(H\otimes H\).
exercises.answer: After the query, the input is \(\tfrac12(\ket{00}+\ket{01}-\ket{10}-\ket{11})=\ket-\ket+\). Applying \(H\otimes H\) gives \(\ket1\ket0\), so the outcome is \(10\), never \(00\). The function is identified as balanced with one query.

exercises.question: With the target in \(\ket-\), the query acts on the input as the phase oracle \(O_f=\mathrm{diag}\big((-1)^{f(0)},(-1)^{f(1)}\big)\). Write \(O_f\) for each of the four functions, and compute \(HO_fH\) in each case. Use the result to describe Deutsch’s algorithm as a single one-qubit operation.
hints: The four phase oracles are \(I\), \(-I\), \(Z\), and \(-Z\).
\(HZH=X\) and \(HIH=I\).
exercises.answer: For \(f=(0,0)\), \(O_f=I\); for \((1,1)\), \(-I\); for \((0,1)\), \(Z\); for \((1,0)\), \(-Z\). Conjugating by \(H\): \(HIH=I\), \(H(-I)H=-I\), \(HZH=X\), and \(H(-Z)H=-X\). So on the input qubit, Deutsch’s algorithm applies \(\pm I\) for a constant function and \(\pm X\) for a balanced one, to the input \(\ket0\). The result is \(\pm\ket0\) or \(\pm\ket1\), and the measurement reads the class with certainty. The signs are global phases, which is why the algorithm cannot reveal which constant or which balanced function was used.

exercises.question: Let \(f(x_1,x_2)=x_1\land x_2\) be computed by a Toffoli gate into an answer bit starting at \(0\). Apply compute, phase, uncompute: Toffoli, then \(Z\) on the answer bit, then Toffoli again. Show that the net operation on \(\ket{x_1x_2}\ket0\) is the controlled-\(Z\) gate on the two inputs, and that the answer bit returns to \(0\).
hints: Track a basis input \(\ket{x_1x_2}\ket0\) through the three steps.
Controlled-\(Z\) multiplies \(\ket{11}\) by \(-1\) and leaves the other basis states alone.
exercises.answer: On \(\ket{x_1x_2}\ket0\), the first Toffoli gate gives \(\ket{x_1x_2}\ket{x_1x_2}\). Then \(Z\) multiplies by \((-1)^{x_1x_2}\). The second Toffoli gate adds \(x_1x_2\) to the answer bit again, returning it to \(0\). The result is \((-1)^{x_1x_2}\ket{x_1x_2}\ket0\): a sign \(-1\) only on \(\ket{11}\), which is controlled-\(Z\), with the answer bit cleanly factored out. By linearity this holds for every superposition of inputs. The phase oracle of AND costs two Toffoli gates and one \(Z\), with one temporary bit, and the clean workspace is what allows the inputs’ signs to interfere later.

exercises.question: A circuit for \(f(x_1,x_2)=x_1\oplus x_2\) first copies \(x_1\) into a workspace bit \(w\), then forms the answer \(w\oplus x_2\). A programmer applies \(Z\) to the answer and uncomputes the answer step only, leaving \(w=x_1\). Starting from the uniform input superposition, apply \(H\) to both inputs and find the outcome distribution. Compare with the clean version.
hints: Before the final Hadamards the state is \(\frac12\sum_x(-1)^{x_1\oplus x_2}\ket{x_1x_2}\ket{x_1}\).
Group the terms by the value of \(w\).
exercises.answer: Group by \(w\). For \(w=0\) the input part is \(\frac12(\ket{00}-\ket{01})=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\ket0\ket-\); for \(w=1\) it is \(\frac12(-\ket{10}+\ket{11})=-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\ket1\ket-\). After \(H\otimes H\) these become \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\ket+\ket1\ket0\) and \(-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\ket-\ket1\ket1\). The second input reads \(1\) with certainty, but the first input is \(\ket+\) on one record and \(\ket-\) on the other, so it reads \(0\) or \(1\) with probability \(\frac12\). The outcomes are \(01\) and \(11\), each with probability \(\frac12\). The clean version gives \(11\) with certainty. The garbage records \(x_1\), so it destroys exactly the interference that would reveal the \(x_1\) part of the answer, while the \(x_2\) part survives.

exercises.question: A student claims: “Deutsch’s algorithm evaluates \(f(0)\) and \(f(1)\) in one query, so with a better readout it could report both values.” Write the full two-qubit output state in terms of \(f(0)\) and \(d=f(0)\oplus f(1)\), and explain why no measurement of it can reveal \(f(0)\).
hints: Factor out \((-1)^{f(0)}\) from the final input amplitudes.
Which part of the state depends on \(f(0)\) alone?
exercises.answer: After the final Hadamard, the input is \(\frac{s_0+s_1}{2}\ket0+\frac{s_0-s_1}{2}\ket1\) with \(s_x=(-1)^{f(x)}\). Factoring out \(s_0\), this is \((-1)^{f(0)}\ket d\), so the output is \((-1)^{f(0)}\ket d\ket-\). The value \(f(0)\) appears only in a global phase, which no measurement detects, and the target \(\ket-\) is the same for every function. So the output carries exactly one bit, \(d\). The query did act on both inputs, but the interference that made \(d\) certain also discarded every other distinction. One query of this kind reveals at most one bit about \(f\), not both values.

exercises.question: Show that Deutsch’s algorithm gives the same outcome for \(f\) and for its complement \(1-f\), and that the outcome depends only on \(f(0)\oplus f(1)\).
hints: Complementing \(f\) multiplies both signs by \(-1\).
The final amplitudes are \((s_0\pm s_1)/2\).
exercises.answer: For \(1-f\), each sign \((-1)^{f(x)}\) is multiplied by \(-1\), a global phase that changes no probability. The outcome is \(1\) exactly when \(s_0\neq s_1\), that is, when \(f(0)\oplus f(1)=1\). The algorithm extracts this one bit and nothing more about \(f\).

exercises.question: A two-bit function is promised to have the form \(f(x)=s_1x_1\oplus s_2x_2\) for an unknown string \(s=s_1s_2\). Run the two-qubit version of the algorithm (Hadamards on both inputs, target \(\ket-\), one query, Hadamards on both inputs) for \(s=10\) and \(s=11\), and show that the measurement returns \(s\). How many classical queries are needed to learn \(s\)?
hints: After the query the input amplitudes are \(\frac12(-1)^{s\cdot x}\).
\((-1)^{s_1x_1}(-1)^{s_2x_2}\) is a product of one-qubit sign patterns.
exercises.answer: After the query the input state is \(\frac12\sum_x(-1)^{s_1x_1}(-1)^{s_2x_2}\ket{x_1x_2}=\frac{\ket0+(-1)^{s_1}\ket1}{\sqrt2}\otimes\frac{\ket0+(-1)^{s_2}\ket1}{\sqrt2}\). Each factor is \(\ket+\) if \(s_i=0\) and \(\ket-\) if \(s_i=1\), and \(H\) maps them to \(\ket0\) and \(\ket1\). So the output is \(\ket{s_1s_2}\) with certainty: \(10\) gives \(\ket{10}\) and \(11\) gives \(\ket{11}\). Classically each query returns one bit, \(s\cdot x\), and there are four possible strings, so two queries are necessary (and \(x=10,01\) suffice). With \(n\) bits the gap is one query against \(n\). This is the Bernstein–Vazirani problem, developed in Quantum Algorithms.

09-amplitude-amplification.purpose: Turn a phase mark into increased success probability and determine when to stop iterating.
09-amplitude-amplification.before: Use phase oracles, reflections, and normalized state vectors.
outcomes: Calculate the four-item search.
Interpret two reflections as a rotation.
Include preparation and oracle costs in amplification.
09-amplitude-amplification.limits: The standard iteration formula assumes ideal reflections and a fixed marked subspace. The best iteration count depends on the initial success probability.
09-amplitude-amplification.example: Start with four equal amplitudes; carry the same reflection picture into the good/bad two-dimensional plane.
09-amplitude-amplification.next: Chapter 10 compares query savings with gate costs and lower bounds.

exercises.question: For \(N=32\) and \(M=2\), find \(\sin\theta\) and the initial success probability.
hints: \(\sin^2\theta=M/N\).
Compare with \(N=16\), \(M=1\).
exercises.answer: \(\sin\theta=\sqrt{2/32}=1/4\), and the initial success probability is \(1/16\), the same as for one marked item among sixteen.

exercises.question: For \(N=8\) with one marked item, find \(\theta\), the number of iterations \(k\) that maximizes the success probability, and that probability. What happens at \(k=3\)?
hints: \(\sin\theta=1/\sqrt8\), so \(\theta\approx0.361\).
exercises.answer: \(\theta=\arcsin(1/\sqrt8)\approx0.361\) rad (about \(20.7^\circ\)), and \(\frac{\pi}{4\theta}-\frac12\approx1.67\), so \(k=2\). The success probabilities for \(k=0,1,2,3\) are about \(0.125,\ 0.781,\ 0.945,\ 0.330\). The best choice gives \(0.945\) with two oracle queries, against a classical guess-and-check that needs about four queries for even a \(50\%\) chance. At \(k=3\) the state has rotated past the good direction, and the success probability falls to \(0.33\).

exercises.question: For \(N=4\) with three marked items, find \(\theta\) and the success probability before and after one Grover iteration. What should a search algorithm do when most items are marked?
hints: \(\sin\theta=\sqrt{3/4}\), so \(\theta=\pi/3\).
After one iteration the angle is \(3\theta\).
exercises.answer: \(\sin\theta=\sqrt3/2\) gives \(\theta=\pi/3\), and the initial success probability is \(\frac34\). One iteration turns the state to \(3\theta=\pi\), so \(p_1=\sin^2\pi=0\): every outcome is unmarked. The state started closer to the good direction than one rotation step, and the rotation overshot completely. When the marked fraction is large, a random guess already succeeds with high probability, so the algorithm should simply sample and check. The randomized schedules of Section 9.3.3 include zero iterations among their choices, which covers this case.

exercises.question: For \(N=32\) and \(M=2\), find the number of Grover iterations that maximizes success, and the success probability.
hints: The angle is the same as for \(N=16\), \(M=1\).
Compute \(\sin^2((2k+1)\theta)\) for \(k=2,3,4\).
exercises.answer: With \(\theta\approx14.48^\circ\), the success probabilities for \(k=2,3,4\) are about \(0.91\), \(0.96\), and \(0.58\). The best is \(k=3\), with success about \(0.96\). Only the marked fraction matters, not \(N\) or \(M\) separately.

exercises.question: A one-qubit preparation \(A\) gives \(A\ket0=\cos\alpha\ket0+\sin\alpha\ket1\) with \(\alpha=\pi/10\), and success means outcome \(1\). (a) Find \(p\) and \(\theta\). (b) How many amplification iterations give certain success? (c) How many independent trials of \(A\) are needed for success probability \(0.99\), and how do the two counts of calls to \(A\) or \(A^\dagger\) compare?
hints: Here \(\theta=\alpha\).
Require \((2k+1)\theta=\pi/2\). Each iteration uses \(A\) and \(A^\dagger\) once.
exercises.answer: (a) \(p=\sin^2(\pi/10)\approx0.0955\) and \(\theta=\pi/10\). (b) \((2k+1)\frac{\pi}{10}=\frac\pi2\) gives \(k=2\), so two iterations succeed with certainty. (c) Independent trials fail with probability \((1-p)^t\le e^{-pt}\). Requiring \(e^{-pt}\le0.01\) gives \(t\ge\ln100/0.0955\approx48\) trials. The amplified version uses one initial \(A\) plus, per iteration, one \(A^\dagger\) and one \(A\): five calls in all, together with two success reflections. A non-uniform preparation is amplified exactly like search, because only the angle \(\theta\) matters.

exercises.question: When \(M\) is unknown, choose the number of iterations \(k\) uniformly from \(\{0,1,2,3\}\). For \(N=16\), compute the average success probability when \(M=1\) and when \(M=4\). Why does a random choice protect against not knowing \(M\)?
hints: For \(M=1\), \(\theta\approx0.2527\); for \(M=4\), \(\theta=\pi/6\).
Average \(\sin^2((2k+1)\theta)\) over the four values of \(k\).
exercises.answer: For \(M=1\), the probabilities for \(k=0,\dots,3\) are about \(0.063,\ 0.473,\ 0.908,\ 0.961\), averaging \(0.60\). For \(M=4\), they are \(0.25,\ 1,\ 0.25,\ 0.25\), averaging \(0.44\). A fixed choice tuned for \(M=1\), namely \(k=3\), would give only \(0.25\) when \(M=4\), and the choice tuned for \(M=4\), \(k=1\), gives \(0.47\) when \(M=1\). Averaged over a range of \(k\), \(\sin^2\) of a steadily advancing angle is close to \(\frac12\) once the range covers about a quarter turn. So each random attempt succeeds with constant probability for every \(M\) in the range, and checking the candidate with one query confirms success. Growing the range gradually keeps the total query count of order \(\sqrt{N/M}\).

exercises.question: Two preparations are available for the same search task, each with a \(20\)-gate success test. \(A_1\) costs \(10\) gates and succeeds with \(p_1=10^{-6}\); \(A_2\) costs \(1000\) gates and succeeds with \(p_2=10^{-3}\). Using the estimate \((C_A+C_G)/p\) for classical repetition and \((2C_A+C_G)/\sqrt p\) for amplitude amplification, compare the costs of both preparations under both strategies.
hints: Compute four numbers and compare within each strategy.
exercises.answer: Classical repetition: \(A_1\) costs \(30\times10^6=3\times10^7\) gates; \(A_2\) costs \(1020\times10^3\approx1.0\times10^6\). The expensive but better preparation wins by a factor of about \(30\). Amplification: \(A_1\) costs \(40\times1000=4\times10^4\); \(A_2\) costs \(2020\times31.6\approx6.4\times10^4\). Now the cheap preparation wins. Amplification takes a square root of \(1/p\) but pays the preparation cost in full each round, so improvements in \(p\) are worth less than they are classically. The best design depends on the whole cost formula, not on the success probability alone.

exercises.question: A student says: “Grover search always finds the marked item with certainty if you choose the right number of iterations.” Test the claim for \(N=16\), \(M=1\). What condition on \(\theta\) would certainty require, and what is known about when it can hold for one marked item?
hints: Certainty requires \((2k+1)\theta=\pi/2\) for some integer \(k\).
For \(N=16\), the best success probability is at \(k=3\).
exercises.answer: For \(N=16\), the success probabilities are about \(0.063,0.473,0.908,0.961,0.582,\dots\), so the best is \(0.961\) at \(k=3\), not \(1\). Certainty needs \((2k+1)\theta=\pi/2\) exactly, that is \(\sin^2\big(\pi/(4k+2)\big)=M/N\). With \(M=1\) the right side is \(1/N\), a rational number. By a theorem of Niven, the only rational values of \(\sin^2\) at rational multiples of \(\pi\) are \(0,\frac14,\frac12,\frac34,1\), so among \(N\ge2\) only \(N=4\) gives certainty with standard iterations. Grover’s algorithm guarantees success probability at least \(1-M/N\) at the best \(k\). Exact success is possible, but it needs modified phases in the final iteration, a technique developed in Quantum Algorithms.

exercises.question: For \(N=4\) with two marked items, show that Grover iterations never change the success probability.
hints: Find \(\theta\) from \(\sin^2\theta=1/2\).
Compute \(\sin^2((2k+1)\theta)\).
exercises.answer: \(\theta=45^\circ\), so the angles \((2k+1)45^\circ\) are odd multiples of \(45^\circ\), and \(\sin^2\) of every one is \(1/2\). Iterating never helps: when half the items are marked, a random guess is already as good as the algorithm can do.

exercises.question: Prove the guarantee behind the stopping rule. Let \(k\) be the integer nearest to \(\frac{\pi}{4\theta}-\frac12\). (a) Show that \((2k+1)\theta\) lies within \(\theta\) of \(\pi/2\). (b) Deduce \(p_k\ge\cos^2\theta=1-M/N\). (c) Show that \(k\le\frac\pi4\sqrt{N/M}\), using \(\theta\ge\sin\theta\).
hints: Rounding changes \(k\) by at most \(\frac12\), so \((2k+1)\theta\) changes by at most \(\theta\).
If an angle \(\varphi\) satisfies \(|\varphi-\pi/2|\le\theta\), then \(\sin^2\varphi\ge\cos^2\theta\).
exercises.answer: (a) Let \(k^*=\frac{\pi}{4\theta}-\frac12\), so \((2k^*+1)\theta=\frac\pi2\) exactly. The nearest integer satisfies \(|k-k^*|\le\frac12\), so \(|(2k+1)\theta-\frac\pi2|=2\theta|k-k^*|\le\theta\). (b) Writing \(\varphi=(2k+1)\theta=\frac\pi2+\delta\) with \(|\delta|\le\theta\), we get \(\sin^2\varphi=\cos^2\delta\ge\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta=1-M/N\), since \(\theta<\pi/2\). (c) \(k\le k^*+\frac12=\frac{\pi}{4\theta}\le\frac{\pi}{4\sin\theta}=\frac\pi4\sqrt{N/M}\). So at most \(\frac\pi4\sqrt{N/M}\) queries achieve success probability at least \(1-M/N\), which is the quantitative form of the quadratic speedup for search.

08-circuits-universality.purpose: Translate abstract operations into circuits and account for the work hidden inside a gate box.
08-circuits-universality.before: Use the query algorithm, phase marking, unitary evolution, and joint-state notation.
outcomes: Read circuit order and controlled operations.
Distinguish exact construction from approximation.
Count gates, depth, and workspace separately.
08-circuits-universality.limits: A finite discrete gate set generally approximates arbitrary unitaries; universality does not imply every transformation has a short exact circuit.
08-circuits-universality.example: Decompose an oracle and a reflection into gates, then use these constructions in the search algorithm that follows.
08-circuits-universality.next: Chapter 9 uses phase oracles and reflections to increase the probability of a marked answer.

exercises.question: Do \(H\) followed by \(Z\), and \(Z\) followed by \(H\), have the same action on \(\ket0\)?
hints: Compute the first step in each order.
\(Z\ket0=\ket0\), but \(Z\ket+=\ket-\).
exercises.answer: No. \(H\) then \(Z\) gives \(\ket-\); \(Z\) then \(H\) gives \(\ket+\). The order of the matrices must follow the order in time.

exercises.question: Compute \(R_Y(\pi/2)=\cos\frac\pi4I-i\sin\frac\pi4Y\) as a matrix. Compare \(R_Y(\pi/2)\ket0\) with \(H\ket0\), and \(R_Y(\pi/2)\ket1\) with \(H\ket1\). Are the two gates the same? Express \(R_Y(\pi/2)\) using \(H\) and one Pauli gate.
hints: \(-iY=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\).
Compare the columns of the two matrices.
exercises.answer: \(R_Y(\pi/2)=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\). On \(\ket0\) both gates give \((\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2\). On \(\ket1\), \(R_Y(\pi/2)\) gives \((-\ket0+\ket1)/\sqrt2=-\ket-\), while \(H\) gives \(\ket-\). The sign is relative to the \(\ket0\) column, so the gates differ: on \(\ket+\), for example, \(R_Y(\pi/2)\) gives \(\ket1\) and \(H\) gives \(\ket0\). In fact \(R_Y(\pi/2)=HZ\): apply \(Z\), then \(H\). Agreement on one input does not identify a gate; a unitary is fixed by its action on every basis state, including phases.

exercises.question: A gate \(V\) equals \(U\) up to the global phase \(i\): \(V=iU\). Apply controlled-\(U\) and controlled-\(V\) to \(\ket+\ket\psi\) and compare the results. What one-qubit gate on the control accounts for the difference?
hints: Controlled-\(V\) applies \(iU\) only on the control-\(1\) branch.
\(S=\mathrm{diag}(1,i)\).
exercises.answer: Controlled-\(U\) gives \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0\ket\psi+\ket1U\ket\psi)\). Controlled-\(V\) gives \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0\ket\psi+i\ket1U\ket\psi)\). The factor \(i\) appears only on the control-\(1\) branch, so it is now a relative phase between branches: controlled-\(V\) equals controlled-\(U\) followed by \(S\) on the control. A phase that is invisible when \(U\) is applied alone becomes observable once \(U\) is controlled, which is why approximations used inside controlled operations must fix the phase, as Section 8.3.3 warns.

exercises.question: Build the complete two-qubit Grover circuit for the marked item \(10\): the oracle from an \(X\) gate and a controlled-\(Z\), and the reflection from \(H\), \(X\), and controlled-\(Z\) gates. Verify that one iteration from \(\ket s\) gives \(10\).
hints: The oracle flips the sign of \(\ket{10}\): apply \(X\) to the qubit that should be \(0\).
The reflection is \(H^{\otimes2}(X\otimes X)\,CZ\,(X\otimes X)H^{\otimes2}\).
exercises.answer: Oracle: \(X\) on qubit 2, controlled-\(Z\), \(X\) on qubit 2. It sends \(\ket{10}\) to \(\ket{11}\), applies the sign, and restores \(\ket{10}\). Starting from \(\ket s=\tfrac12(1,1,1,1)\), the oracle gives \(\tfrac12(1,1,-1,1)\). The reflection circuit implements \(-D\), and \(D\) maps this state to \(\ket{10}\), so the result is \(-\ket{10}\): the outcome is \(10\) with certainty.

exercises.question: Show that the reflection \(D=2\ket s\bra s-I\) about the uniform state acts on amplitudes as “inversion about the mean”: if \(\ket\psi=\sum_xa_x\ket x\) and \(\bar a\) is the average of the \(a_x\), then \(D\ket\psi=\sum_x(2\bar a-a_x)\ket x\). Use it to redo one Grover iteration on two qubits with marked item \(10\).
hints: \(\braket s\psi=\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_xa_x=\sqrt N\,\bar a\).
After the oracle, the amplitudes are \(\frac12,\frac12,-\frac12,\frac12\).
exercises.answer: Since \(\braket s\psi=\sqrt N\,\bar a\), we have \(2\ket s\braket s\psi=2\sqrt N\,\bar a\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_x\ket x=\sum_x2\bar a\ket x\). Subtracting \(\ket\psi\) gives amplitudes \(2\bar a-a_x\): each amplitude is reflected about the mean. For two qubits, \(\ket s\) has all amplitudes \(\frac12\). The oracle for \(10\) makes them \(\frac12,\frac12,-\frac12,\frac12\), with mean \(\frac14\). Reflecting gives \(2\cdot\frac14-\frac12=0\) for the three unmarked items and \(2\cdot\frac14+\frac12=1\) for \(10\). One iteration finds the marked item with certainty. The negative amplitude lies far below the mean, so the reflection throws it far above.

exercises.question: On two qubits, build the phase oracle \((-1)^{x_1\lor x_2}\) for OR. (a) Show that \(X\otimes X\), then controlled-\(Z\), then \(X\otimes X\), multiplies only \(\ket{00}\) by \(-1\). (b) Explain why this circuit implements the OR phase oracle up to a global phase. (c) When would that global phase matter?
hints: \(X\otimes X\) maps \(\ket{00}\) to \(\ket{11}\), the only state that controlled-\(Z\) changes.
Compare the sign patterns \((-,+,+,+)\) and \((+,-,-,-)\).
exercises.answer: (a) \(X\otimes X\) sends \(\ket{00}\) to \(\ket{11}\), controlled-\(Z\) multiplies it by \(-1\), and \(X\otimes X\) returns it to \(\ket{00}\). Every other basis state is mapped away from \(\ket{11}\) and back without a sign. So the circuit has signs \((-,+,+,+)\) on \(00,01,10,11\). (b) OR is \(0\) only on \(00\), so its phase oracle has signs \((+,-,-,-)\), exactly \(-1\) times the circuit. Used by itself, as in a search iteration, the factor \(-1\) multiplies the whole state and changes no probability. (c) If the oracle is controlled by another qubit, the \(-1\) acts only on the control-\(1\) branch and becomes a \(Z\) on the control, so the correct sign must be restored, for example by a \(Z\) on that control.

exercises.question: Grover search over \(N=2^{20}\) items uses about \((\pi/4)\sqrt N\) iterations, each compiled into \(300\) elementary gates. (a) Estimate the total gate count. (b) If each gate fails independently with probability \(10^{-4}\), estimate the probability that the whole circuit runs without a failure. (c) What failure probability per gate would give at least \(0.9\)?
hints: \((1-p)^G\approx e^{-pG}\) for small \(p\).
exercises.answer: (a) About \(\frac\pi4\times1024\approx804\) iterations, so roughly \(804\times300\approx2.4\times10^5\) gates.
